Even though the ideals are distinct if κ is uncountable but not inaccessible, it is an open question whether the cardinal invariants given by the combinatorial κ -meagre ideal are consistently distinct from those given by the topological κ -meagre ideal:

Question 2.3. Let the combinatorially κ -meagre ideal M comb κ be defined as in [BHZ, Def. 4.4]. Is non( M comb κ ) < non( M κ ) or cov( M κ ) < cov( M comb κ ) consistent for κ that are not inaccessible?

The characterisation of cof( N ) and add( N ) from Theorem 2.1 cannot be generalised to the higher context, not just because we would need a higher analogue of N , but also because the cardinality of d h κ ( ∈ ∗ ) is highly dependent on the choice of h ∈ κ κ when κ is inaccessible, as we will discuss in Section 3.2. For successor κ , Theorem 2.1 looks very different:

Theorem 2.4 ([Hyt06], [MS, Thm. 4.6]) . If κ is a regular successor, then b κ ( ✟ ✟ = ∞ ) = b h κ ( ∈ ∗ ) = b κ and d κ = d h κ ( ∈ ∗ ) ≥ d κ ( ✟ ✟ = ∞ ) . If we also assume κ <κ = κ , then the last inequality becomes an equality.

Question 2.5 ([MS, § 4]) . Is d κ ( ✟ ✟ = ∞ ) < d κ consistent for κ a successor cardinal and κ <κ > κ ?

It was observed by Truss and Miller that the cardinal characteristics add( M ) and cof( M ) can be expressed in terms of the other cardinals of the Cicho´ n diagram.

Theorem 2.6 ([Tru77], [Mil81]) . add( M ) = min { b , cov( M ) } and cof( M ) = max { d , non( M ) } .

The same characterisation generalises to the higher Cicho´ n diagram if we make strong enough assumptions on κ . We note that this is not provable for all uncountable κ . For example, Brendle [Bre22] showed that κ <κ < cof( M κ ), and thus max { d κ , non( M κ ) } < cof( M κ ) is consistent, and holds whenever max { d κ , non( M κ ) } ≤ κ <κ .

Theorem 2.7 ([Bre22]) . add( M κ ) = min { b κ , cov( M κ ) } and cof( M κ ) ≥ max { d κ , non( M κ ) } . Under assumption of κ <κ = κ the inequality becomes an equality.

As for the other eight cardinal characteristics of the classical Cicho´ n diagram, they appear to be as independent as is possible in the following sense: any assignment of the cardinalities ℵ 1 and ℵ 2 to the cardinals of the classical Cicho´ n diagram compatible with both Theorem 2.6 and the arrows in the diagram, is consistent (see [BJ95, Sections 7.5 and 7.6] for each of these cases). This implies that the classical Cicho´ n diagram is complete, as no arrows are missing from the diagram. In fact, Goldstern, Kellner, Mej´ ıa, and Shelah [GKMS21; GKS19] showed that all eight cardinal characteristics can have mutually different cardinalities within the same model.
